quests.d: What a rate limiter is, why you need one, how to scope it, and where it should sit
quests.goal: Your win today: you can explain in one breath what a rate limiter does, give three reasons to have one, ask the five scoping questions, and defend where you'd put it (middleware or API gateway, not the client).
quests.bookSections: Ch. 4 intro (benefits of an API rate limiter); Step 1 (understand the problem: candidate/interviewer dialogue + requirements); Step 2 'Where to put the rate limiter?' including API gateway and the build-vs-buy guidelines; Step 4 wrap-up point on rate limiting at different OSI layers

stages.title: Why bounce anyone?
stages.sub: Three reasons every big API has a limiter
stages.teaches: Definition: in a network system, a rate limiter controls the rate of traffic a client or a service sends. For HTTP it limits how many requests a client may send in a time period; requests over the threshold are blocked. Book examples of rules: a user can write no more than 2 posts per second; at most 10 accounts per day from the same IP address; rewards can be claimed no more than 5 times per week from the same device. Three benefits from the book: (1) Prevent resource starvation caused by a Denial of Service (DoS) attack, meaning flooding a service so real users can't get in. Almost every big tech API has limits; the book cites Twitter capping tweets at 300 per 3 hours and the Google Docs API defaulting to 300 read requests per user per 60 seconds. (2) Reduce cost: fewer excess requests means fewer servers, and capacity goes to high-priority APIs. This matters most when you pay per call to a third-party API (checking credit, making a payment, retrieving health records). (3) Prevent servers from being overloaded by bots or users' misbehavior.
stages.interaction: 'Sort the incident' card game. Six incident cards appear one at a time, for example: 'A script tries 50,000 passwords per minute on /login'; 'A buggy mobile release retries every failed call in a tight loop'; 'Your bill from the credit-check vendor tripled overnight'; 'A scraper bot crawls every product page 20 times a second'; 'Free-tier users' batch jobs crowd out paying customers'; 'A botnet sends 2 Tbps of junk UDP packets at your data center'. The learner taps one of three bins: Starvation (DoS), Cost, Overload. Correct = +XP and the card flies into the bin; wrong = shake + one-line explanation. The botnet card's correct bin is a fourth hidden option revealed on tap of any bin: 'Not the limiter's job' — the explanation says an HTTP rate limiter can't absorb a volumetric network flood; that needs network-level DDoS protection upstream. End with Q.quiz: 'Which is NOT one of the book's three benefits?' (options: prevent resource starvation / reduce cost / prevent server overload / guarantee every request is answered within 100 ms — correct is the last).
stages.check: Q.quiz on the three benefits; the card sort must be completed (all six cards placed) to clear the stage.

stages.title: Scope it in five questions
stages.sub: Step 1: what the interviewer actually wants
stages.teaches: The book's scoping dialogue and its answers: client-side or server-side? Server-side API rate limiter. Throttle by IP, user ID, or something else? Flexible enough to support different sets of throttle rules. Scale? Must handle a large number of requests (startup or big company). Distributed environment? Yes. Separate service or inside application code? Design decision up to you. Inform throttled users? Yes. Resulting requirements (six): accurately limit excessive requests; low latency (must not slow down HTTP response time); use as little memory as possible; distributed rate limiting (one limiter shared across many servers or processes); exception handling (show clear exceptions to throttled users); high fault tolerance (if the limiter has a problem, e.g. a cache server goes offline, it must not take down the whole system).
stages.interaction: Chat-style interview. A deck of 9 question cards: 6 good ones (the book's six questions) and 3 time-wasters ('Which frontend framework do you use?', 'What color should the error page be?', 'Should we run it on Kubernetes?'). Tapping a good question appends the interviewer's answer to the chat and pins a requirement card onto a 'Requirements board' (6 slots). Tapping a time-waster costs one heart and the interviewer replies 'Let's not go there yet.' When the board is full, a mini-match: the learner drags each of the six requirement names onto a one-line consequence ('one cache outage must not 500 every API' → high fault tolerance; 'adds no noticeable time to each call' → low latency; 'two servers must agree on one user's count' → distributed; etc.).
stages.check: All six requirement cards pinned and matched; Q.quiz: 'The interviewer says the limiter must keep working when a cache node dies. Which requirement is that?' → high fault tolerance.

stages.title: Where does the bouncer stand?
stages.sub: Client, server, or middleware — predict, then watch
stages.teaches: Client-side limiting is unreliable: client requests can easily be forged by malicious actors, and you may not control the client implementation. Server-side: inside the API servers. Middleware: a separate rate limiter that sits between client and API servers and throttles requests before they reach them. Book example: API allows 2 requests per second; a client sends 3 within one second; the first two are routed to API servers, the third is rejected with HTTP status 429 Too Many Requests. API gateway: a fully managed service (cloud) that supports rate limiting plus SSL termination, authentication, IP whitelisting, serving static content. In a microservice architecture, the limiter usually lives in the API gateway. Also (from wrap-up): you can limit at different OSI layers — the book's design limits at the application layer (HTTP, layer 7); you can also limit by IP address with iptables at the network layer (IP, layer 3).
stages.interaction: Diagram sim: Client → [slot A] → [slot B: middleware] → API servers [slot C inside]. A rate limiter token can be dragged into slot A (in client), B (middleware), or C (inside API server). Rule: 2 requests/second. Before pressing 'Send 3 requests in 1 second', the learner predicts how many reach the API servers (input 0–3). Watch: packets animate; with B or C, 2 pass and the 3rd bounces back red with '429'. Then a toggle 'Attacker patches the app' appears: with the limiter in slot A, all 3 (then 30) requests reach the servers because the attacker removed the client check; with B the attacker still gets 429s. Correct predictions = XP. Then a callout box shows the layer-3 vs layer-7 idea with a tiny OSI ladder (7 Application … 3 Network) highlighting where the book's limiter (L7) and iptables (L3) act.
stages.check: Predict-then-watch scored (2 reach the servers); Q.quiz: 'Why is a client-side rate limiter not enough?' → requests can be forged / you don't control the client.

stages.title: Build it or buy it?
stages.teaches: No absolute answer; it depends on the company's tech stack, engineering resources, priorities, goals. Book guidelines: (1) evaluate your current tech stack (programming language, cache service) and make sure the language is efficient enough to implement rate limiting on the server side; (2) pick a rate limiting algorithm that fits business needs — implementing it yourself gives full control, a third-party gateway may limit your choice of algorithm; (3) if you already use microservices with an API gateway (doing authentication, IP whitelisting, etc.), you may add the limiter to the gateway; (4) building your own takes time — if you lack engineering resources, a commercial API gateway is a better option.
stages.interaction: Four company profile cards, one at a time. Learner chooses 'Build my own middleware' or 'Use the API gateway' and then picks the guideline that justifies it from 4 chips. Profiles: (a) 3-person startup already on a cloud API gateway with auth there → gateway, guideline 3/4; (b) fintech that needs a custom per-merchant sliding-window rule the vendor gateway doesn't offer → build, guideline 2; (c) team of 40 with an in-house Redis cluster and Go services, wants full control → build, guideline 1/2; (d) small team, tight deadline, no gateway yet → buy a commercial gateway, guideline 4. Both the choice and the justification must be right for full XP; choice right but justification wrong = half XP.
stages.check: All four profiles answered; quiz: 'A third-party API gateway's main downside per the book?' → it may limit your choice of algorithm.

stages.title: Boss: The Gatecrasher
stages.teaches: Applies stages 1–4 to tricky cases, plus: limiting by IP hurts users behind NAT (a whole office or mobile carrier shares one public IP), so key by user ID or API key when users are authenticated; the 429 status code; limits at different layers.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 5 scenarios, 3 choices each. Examples: 'The PM says we can just rate-limit inside the mobile app. You say…' (correct: server-side too, clients can be forged); 'Throttled requests should get which HTTP status?' (429 / 503 / 403 → 429); 'All 2,000 employees of a customer share one office IP and get blocked together. Fix?' (key the limit on user ID / API key); 'You already route all traffic through an API gateway doing auth. Where does the limiter go?' (the gateway); 'Interviewer: what does the limiter do when its own cache is down?' (choices: block everything / let traffic through and alert / crash — correct: let traffic through and alert, tying to the high-fault-tolerance requirement; explanation flags this is a choice called failing open, revisited in 4.5).
stages.check: Boss defeated (engine rules).

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Pulls it together into an interview answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'The interviewer asks: why do we need a rate limiter, and where would you put it?' Model answer mentions: limits requests per client per window, returns 429; three benefits (DoS/starvation, cost, overload); server-side because clients can be forged; as middleware or in the API gateway if one exists; choice depends on stack and team resources. Checks: mentions 429; names at least two benefits; rejects client-side with the reason; names middleware or API gateway; mentions a trade-off (control vs time/resources).
stages.check: Self-graded drill completed.

caveats: The book's example limits (Twitter 300 tweets per 3 hours, Google Docs 300 reads per user per 60 s) were real when written but platform limits change often; treat them as illustrations, not current facts.

An HTTP rate limiter does not stop a large network-level DDoS: by the time a request is parsed as HTTP, the bandwidth is already spent. Real systems layer network DDoS protection (often at the CDN or edge) in front.
Rate-limiting by IP is blunt: many users can share one IP (offices, mobile carriers using NAT), and attackers can rotate IPs. Prefer user ID or API key when requests are authenticated.
Client-side limiting is still worth having as politeness (fewer wasted calls), just never as the only protection.

quests.d: The two bucket algorithms: token bucket and leaking bucket
quests.goal: Your win today: you can run the token bucket and leaking bucket in your head, name their two parameters each, say who uses them (Amazon, Stripe; Shopify), and pick the right one for 'allow bursts' vs 'smooth steady output'.
quests.bookSections: Step 2 'Algorithms for rate limiting': token bucket and leaking bucket (with pros/cons); wrap-up point on hard vs soft rate limiting

stages.title: Fill the bucket
stages.teaches: Token bucket: a container with a pre-defined capacity. A refiller puts tokens in at a preset rate; once the bucket is full, extra tokens overflow (are lost). Each request consumes one token. If there is a token, take it and let the request through; if not, the request is dropped. Book figure: bucket size 4, refill rate 4 per minute. Two parameters: bucket size (max tokens = the biggest burst allowed) and refill rate (tokens added per second = the long-run average rate). Because a full bucket can be spent at once, it allows short bursts of traffic.
stages.interaction: Live sim. A bucket drawn with 4 token slots, starting full. Game time is sped up (1 real second = 15 game seconds, so the refill of 4/min shows as 1 token every real second; a speed toggle offers 1× and paused). Buttons: 'Send 1 request' and 'Send burst of 5'. Each request is a packet that grabs a token (token disappears, packet goes green to 'API') or, with an empty bucket, bounces red ('dropped'). Overflow tokens visibly spill over the rim when the bucket is full. Counters: allowed / dropped / tokens now. Two mini-challenges with checkmarks: (1) 'Get 4 requests through in one instant' (burst while full); (2) 'Get a request dropped, then get one through again without sending a burst' (wait for refill).
stages.check: Both challenges completed; quiz: 'Which parameter sets the biggest burst you allow?' → bucket size.

stages.title: Predict the drops
stages.sub: Calculate, then watch the bucket do it
stages.teaches: Real implementations don't run a refiller timer per bucket; they store two numbers (tokens left, time of last refill) and on each request compute tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate), then try to take one. This is cheap and exact.
stages.interaction: Three calculate-and-check rounds using the formula. Each shows a timeline of request arrivals; the learner types how many are dropped, then presses 'Watch' and the sim replays it with a running token count. Round 1: capacity 4, refill 1 token per 15 s, starts full; 6 requests at t=0 → 2 dropped. Round 2: same bucket; 6 requests at t=0, then 3 requests at t=30 s → t=0: 4 allowed, 2 dropped; t=30: 2 tokens refilled, 2 allowed, 1 dropped → 3 dropped total. Round 3: capacity 10, refill 2/s, starts with 0 tokens at t=0; 1 request every 0.25 s for 3 s (12 requests, at t=0.25…3.0) → tokens arrive 2/s; by the end about 6 tokens are earned, so ~6 allowed, 6 dropped (accept ±1 and explain the steady state: long-run you get the refill rate, not the burst size). A 'show formula' toggle displays tokens = min(cap, tokens + Δt × rate) per step.
stages.check: At least 2 of 3 rounds correct to earn full XP (all rounds must be attempted to clear).

stages.title: How many buckets?
stages.sub: One bucket per rule, per key
stages.teaches: Book: it is usually necessary to have different buckets for different API endpoints. If a user may make 1 post per second, add 150 friends per day, and like 5 posts per second, that user needs 3 buckets. If you throttle by IP address, each IP address needs a bucket. If the whole system allows a max of 10,000 requests per second, a global bucket shared by all requests makes sense. Pros (book): easy to implement; memory efficient; allows bursts of traffic for short periods as long as tokens are left. Cons: two parameters (bucket size, refill rate) can be hard to tune. Used by Amazon (API Gateway throttling) and Stripe. Hard vs soft rate limiting (wrap-up): hard = requests can never exceed the threshold; soft = requests can exceed the threshold for a short period. A token bucket with a big bucket behaves 'softer' over short windows.
stages.interaction: Bucket counter calc-and-check. A rules panel lists: post 1/sec per user, add friend 150/day per user, like 5/sec per user, plus a global 10,000 req/s. Round 1: 'How many buckets for 1 user?' → 3 user buckets (+1 global shared). Round 2: '1,000 active users?' → 3,000 + 1 global = 3,001. Round 3: 'Switch the login rule to per-IP; 5,000 distinct IPs hit /login' → 5,000 more buckets. Each correct answer animates a grid of tiny buckets filling the panel. Then a hard/soft toggle demo: two meters side by side, limit 10/min — hard meter turns red exactly at 11th, soft meter lets 12 through and then clamps; the learner labels which is which.
stages.check: Rounds answered; quiz: 'Token bucket's main con per the book?' → two parameters that are hard to tune.

stages.title: The leaking bucket
stages.teaches: Leaking bucket: like token bucket but requests are processed at a fixed rate. Usually built with a FIFO (first-in, first-out) queue. A request arrives → if the queue isn't full, it's added; if full, it's dropped. Requests are pulled from the queue and processed at regular intervals. Two parameters: bucket size (= queue size) and outflow rate (requests processed per second). Shopify uses leaky buckets. Pros: memory efficient given the limited queue size; requests processed at a fixed rate, good when you need a stable outflow. Cons: a burst fills the queue with old requests, and if they aren't processed in time, recent requests get rate limited; two parameters are hard to tune.
stages.interaction: Side-by-side predict-then-watch. Left: token bucket (size 4, refill 1/s). Right: leaking bucket (queue 4, outflow 1/s). Learner presses 'Burst of 8 at t=0'. Before watching, predict for each: how many get answered within the first second? (token: 4; leaky: 1) and how many are dropped? (token: 4; leaky: 4 — 4 queued, 4 dropped). Watch: token bucket sends 4 through at once; leaky bucket queues 4 and drips them out one per second while dropping the rest. Then at t=1.5 s a gold 'VIP fresh request' arrives: on the left it waits for a token (bounced if none); on the right it bounces because the queue is still full of old requests — illustrating the 'old requests starve new ones' con.
stages.check: Both predictions entered and compared; quiz: 'You call a downstream payment processor that can only take exactly 10 calls a second, steady. Which bucket?' → leaking bucket.

stages.title: Boss: The Burst Hydra
stages.sub: Pick the bucket, tune the knobs
stages.teaches: Choosing between the buckets and their parameters.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 5 scenarios, 2–3 choices. Examples: 'Public API; users open the app and fire 10 calls at once, then go quiet' → token bucket (allows short bursts); 'Writes into a legacy database that falls over above 50 writes/s' → leaking bucket (steady outflow); 'Users complain a burst of 100 at app launch gets throttled even though their hourly average is low; you use token bucket. Which knob?' → raise bucket size (not refill rate); 'Your average rate is too high overall, bursts are fine. Which knob?' → lower refill rate; 'A limit must never be exceeded, not even for a moment (e.g. a contractual cap). Hard or soft?' → hard.
stages.check: Boss defeated.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Interview-ready comparison.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Compare token bucket and leaking bucket, and tell me when you'd use each.' Model answer: token bucket — tokens refill at a rate up to a capacity, each request takes one, allows bursts up to capacity, params bucket size + refill rate, used by Amazon/Stripe; leaking bucket — FIFO queue drained at a fixed rate, params queue size + outflow rate, smooth output, bursts fill the queue with old requests; choose token for bursty user traffic, leaky when the downstream needs a steady rate. Checks: both parameter pairs named; burst behavior contrasted; one use case each; one con each.
stages.check: Self-graded drill completed.

caveats: The book's 'refiller' that adds tokens on a timer is a mental model. Production limiters (e.g. Stripe's Redis-based one) compute refills lazily from the last timestamp on each request.

There are two 'leaky bucket' ideas: leaky bucket as a queue (the book's version, which delays requests) and leaky bucket as a meter, which rejects instead of queueing and is mathematically equivalent to a token bucket (also known as GCRA). Shopify's API limits are meter-style: over-limit calls get a 429, they are not queued.
Amazon's 'token bucket' here specifically means API Gateway request throttling; it isn't a claim about every Amazon system.

quests.d: Fixed window, sliding window log, and sliding window counter
quests.goal: Your win today: you can show the fixed-window edge exploit (10 requests through a 5/min limit), walk the sliding-log example step by step, compute a sliding-window-counter estimate (3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5) and compare all five algorithms on accuracy, memory and bursts.
quests.bookSections: Step 2 'Algorithms for rate limiting': fixed window counter, sliding window log, sliding window counter (with pros/cons and the Cloudflare figure)

stages.title: Exploit the edge
stages.sub: Fixed window counter and its loophole
stages.teaches: Fixed window counter: divide the timeline into fixed-size windows and keep a counter per window. Each request increments the counter by one; once it reaches the threshold, new requests are dropped until the next window starts. Book example 1: window = 1 second, max 3 requests per second. Problem: a burst at the window edges lets more than the quota through. Book example 2: max 5 requests per minute, quota resets at the round minute; 5 requests between 2:00:00 and 2:01:00 and 5 more between 2:01:00 and 2:02:00 — but the one-minute span 2:00:30–2:01:30 contains 10 requests, twice the limit. Pros: memory efficient; easy to understand; resetting quota at the end of a unit fits some use cases. Cons: spikes at window edges can let through more than the quota.
stages.interaction: Timeline sim from 2:00:00 to 2:02:00, split into two 1-minute windows with counters (limit 5/min). The learner taps on the timeline to drop requests at chosen times; each one shows green (allowed) or red (dropped) and the window's counter increments. A draggable 60-second 'ruler' (a translucent band) can slide anywhere; it shows how many allowed requests fall inside it. Challenge: 'Get 10 allowed requests inside one 60-second ruler position.' Success requires placing ~5 late in window 1 and ~5 early in window 2. On success, the ruler snaps to 2:00:30–2:01:30 and the book's caption appears. A 'Show me' button auto-plays the book example for anyone stuck (no XP).
stages.check: Challenge solved or auto-played; quiz: 'Limit 5/min, fixed windows. Max requests that can pass in some 60-second span?' → 10.

stages.title: Keep a log
stages.sub: Sliding window log, step by step
stages.teaches: Sliding window log fixes the edge problem by tracking each request's timestamp, usually in a cache such as a Redis sorted set (a set ordered by a score — here the timestamp). On a new request: remove all timestamps older than the start of the current window (now − window length); add the new request's timestamp to the log; if the log size is ≤ the allowed count, accept, otherwise reject. Book example (limit 2 requests per minute): 1:00:01 — log empty, accepted. 1:00:30 — log size 2, accepted. 1:00:50 — log size 3 > 2, rejected, but its timestamp stays in the log. 1:01:40 — window is [1:00:40, 1:01:40); 1:00:01 and 1:00:30 are outdated and removed; log is [1:00:50, 1:01:40], size 2 → accepted. Pros: very accurate — in any rolling window, requests never exceed the limit. Cons: lots of memory, since it stores a timestamp per request, even rejected ones.
stages.interaction: Step-through predict game. A log panel (vertical list of timestamp chips) and a clock. For each of the four book requests, the learner first taps 'Accept' or 'Reject', then the sim plays the three steps visibly: grey out and remove expired chips, add the new chip, compare size vs limit. Correct predictions earn XP. On request 3, a highlighted note shows the rejected chip staying in the log. On request 4, the learner must also tap which chips will be evicted (1:00:01 and 1:00:30) before the animation. Finally a memory meter: 'Limit 500/hour, 1M users, each timestamp ~8 bytes' → learner computes worst-case log memory ≈ 500 × 8 B × 1M = 4 GB (accept 3.5–4.5 GB), to make the memory con concrete.
stages.check: Four predictions + the eviction pick + the memory estimate; quiz: 'Why does the log use more memory than it seems to need?' → it stores timestamps even for rejected requests.

stages.title: Blend two windows
stages.sub: Sliding window counter: calculate and check
stages.teaches: Sliding window counter is a hybrid of fixed window counter and sliding log. Estimate requests in the rolling window = requests in current window + requests in previous window × overlap percentage of the rolling window and the previous window. Book example: limit 7 per minute, 5 requests in the previous minute, 3 in the current; a new request arrives 30% into the current minute → 3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5, rounded down to 6 (round up or down depending on the use case) → under 7, so the request goes through; the limit will be reached after one more. Pros: smooths spikes because the rate uses the average of the previous window; memory efficient (two counters per key). Cons: only works for a not-so-strict look-back window; it is an approximation that assumes requests in the previous window were evenly spread. Cloudflare's experiments: only 0.003% of requests were wrongly allowed or rate limited among 400 million requests.
stages.interaction: Slider calculator. A bar shows the previous window (5 requests) and current window (3 requests) with a 60-second rolling band whose position is controlled by a slider (0–100% into the current minute). Live readout: overlap % with previous = 100 − position; estimate = current + previous × overlap. Then 4 calculate-and-check rounds where the learner types the estimate and Allow/Reject (rule shown: round down; allow if estimate < limit): R1 book example (limit 7, prev 5, cur 3, 30%) → 6.5 → 6 → allow. R2 limit 10, prev 8, cur 4, 25% → 4 + 8×0.75 = 10 → reject. R3 limit 10, prev 8, cur 4, 75% → 4 + 2 = 6 → allow. R4 limit 100, prev 120, cur 30, 50% → 30 + 60 = 90 → allow. After R4, a 'What if' card: previous window's 5 requests all came in its last second — the estimate still says 3.5, but reality had 5 in the rolling window: the approximation's blind spot.
stages.check: At least 3 of 4 rounds correct for full XP; quiz: 'What does sliding window counter assume about the previous window?' → its requests were evenly distributed.

stages.title: The algorithm draft
stages.teaches: Summary from the book: token bucket (easy, memory efficient, allows bursts; two params hard to tune; Amazon, Stripe). Leaking bucket (memory efficient, fixed outflow; bursts fill the queue with old requests, two params; Shopify). Fixed window counter (memory efficient, easy, resets at round times; edge spikes). Sliding window log (very accurate; memory hungry). Sliding window counter (smooths spikes, memory efficient; approximate, assumes even distribution).
stages.interaction: Matching board: 5 algorithm columns; 10 shuffled trait cards (each algorithm's main pro and main con). The learner taps a card then a column. Wrong placements shake and cost no heart but no XP for that card. When done, the board turns into a reference table that stays visible. Then a 'Which would you pick?' mini-round with 3 one-line situations: 'must be exact, small user base' → sliding window log; 'billions of keys, approximate is fine' → sliding window counter; 'quota resets at midnight for a daily plan' → fixed window.
stages.check: Board complete; three picks answered.

stages.title: Boss: The Clock Wraith
stages.teaches: Applying the window algorithms under interview pressure.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 5 scenarios. Examples: 'A user gets 2× their per-minute quota through by timing calls around :00. Which algorithm are you on?' → fixed window counter; 'Fix it with the least memory' → sliding window counter (not sliding log); 'Auditors require that no rolling 60-second span ever exceeds the limit' → sliding window log; 'Sliding log memory exploded during an attack. Why?' → rejected requests are still logged; 'Cloudflare's sliding window counter was wrong for what share of 400M requests?' → 0.003%.
stages.check: Boss defeated.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Interview-ready comparison of the three window algorithms.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Walk me through fixed window, sliding log, and sliding window counter — and which you'd ship.' Model answer: fixed window counts per round window, cheap, but edges allow 2× (5/min → 10 in 2:00:30–2:01:30); sliding log stores timestamps in a sorted set, exact, but memory-heavy including rejected ones; sliding window counter = current + previous × overlap (3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5), two counters per key, approximate (Cloudflare 0.003% error); ship sliding window counter or token bucket for most APIs, sliding log when exactness matters and volumes are small. Checks: edge problem with numbers; log memory con; the formula; a reasoned pick.
stages.check: Self-graded drill completed.

caveats: The book says round 6.5 'down' in its example but notes you could round either way; real implementations vary (Cloudflare compares the unrounded weighted rate to the limit).
The 0.003% figure comes from Cloudflare's own traffic; other traffic shapes (very bursty clients) can make the approximation worse.

The book's sliding log adds a rejected request's timestamp to the log. Some implementations only log accepted requests, which saves memory but means a client that keeps hammering isn't penalized for the rejected attempts.

quests.d: Redis counters, rule files, 429 headers, and the detailed design
quests.goal: Your win today: you can explain why counters live in Redis (INCR, EXPIRE), write a Lyft-style rule, list the three rate-limit headers and what the client should do with a 429, and draw the book's detailed design from memory.
quests.bookSections: Step 2 'High-level architecture' (Redis, INCR, EXPIRE); Step 3 deep dive: rate limiting rules, exceeding the rate limit, rate limiter headers, detailed design; Step 4 wrap-up point on client best practices

stages.title: Where do counters live?
stages.teaches: Basic idea of every algorithm: keep a counter of how many requests came from the same user, IP, etc.; if it exceeds the limit, disallow. Store counters in an in-memory cache, not a database: databases are slow because of disk access; an in-memory cache is fast and supports time-based expiration. Redis is the popular choice. Two commands: INCR increases the stored counter by 1; EXPIRE sets a timeout so the counter is deleted automatically. Flow: client → rate limiting middleware; middleware fetches the counter from the corresponding bucket in Redis and checks whether the limit is reached; if reached, reject; if not, send the request to API servers, increment the counter and save it back to Redis.
stages.interaction: Redis console sim. Left: a client button 'Send request'. Right: a Redis key panel showing key 'rl:user42:14:03' (user + current minute), its value and a TTL countdown. Limit 5/min. Each send runs the shown commands with a typing effect (INCR rl:user42:14:03 → 1; EXPIRE … 60 on first increment). The 6th request returns 429. Then 'Spot the bug': a code card shows `n = INCR key; if n > LIMIT: reject; EXPIRE key 60` and a 'kill server' button. The learner presses it between INCR and EXPIRE, then advances the clock 2 minutes: the key never expires and the user is locked out forever. The learner picks the fix from 3 options: (a) run INCR+EXPIRE atomically (MULTI transaction or Lua script) or only call EXPIRE when INCR returns 1 inside one script — correct; (b) increase the TTL; (c) store counters in MySQL.
stages.check: Fix chosen; quiz: 'Why Redis and not the database for counters?' → in-memory is fast + built-in expiration.

stages.title: Write the rules
stages.teaches: Lyft open-sourced its rate-limiting component; rules are written in configuration files and saved on disk. Book example 1: domain: messaging; descriptor key: message_type, value: marketing; rate_limit unit: day, requests_per_unit: 5 — at most 5 marketing messages per day. Example 2: domain: auth; key: auth_type, value: login; unit: minute, requests_per_unit: 5 — clients can't log in more than 5 times in 1 minute.
stages.interaction: YAML builder. Three English rules are presented one at a time: (1) 'No more than 5 marketing messages per day' (book), (2) 'No more than 5 logins per minute' (book), (3) a new one: 'No more than 100 search requests per hour'. A YAML skeleton has dropdown blanks for domain, key, value, unit (second/minute/hour/day), requests_per_unit. Once filled correctly the YAML turns green and a 'Test it' button fires 6 (or 101) simulated events; the last one bounces with 429. Wrong unit is the common trap and gets a hint ('per day ≠ per minute').
stages.check: All three rules built and tested.

stages.title: Tell the client
stages.sub: 429, headers, and how a good client backs off
stages.teaches: When a request is rate limited, the API returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Depending on the use case, rate-limited requests may instead be enqueued to process later (e.g. orders rate limited due to system overload). The client learns its status from headers: X-Ratelimit-Remaining (remaining allowed requests in the window), X-Ratelimit-Limit (how many calls the client can make per window), X-Ratelimit-Retry-After (seconds to wait before retrying without being throttled). On a 429, X-Ratelimit-Retry-After is returned. Client best practices (book wrap-up): use a client cache to avoid frequent API calls; understand the limit and don't send too many requests in a short time; catch exceptions/errors so the client recovers gracefully; add sufficient back-off time to retry logic.
stages.interaction: HTTP response inspector. Limit 5 per minute. The learner steps through 6 requests at t = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 s. For each response, they fill in a small form: status code (200/429), X-Ratelimit-Limit, X-Ratelimit-Remaining, and on the 429 X-Ratelimit-Retry-After (window resets at t=60 → 35). Correct fields light green. Then a 'Client behavior' mini-sim: a client that retries instantly on 429 vs one that waits Retry-After plus random jitter; a counter shows wasted requests (instant retry: dozens; backoff: 0). Learner taps the 4 best-practice cards that are real from 6 (two distractors: 'retry immediately in a loop', 'open more connections to go faster').
stages.check: All six responses correct (hints allowed); best-practice pick correct.

stages.title: Draw the detailed design
stages.teaches: Book's detailed design: rules are stored on disk; workers frequently pull rules from disk and store them in the cache. A client request goes to the rate limiter middleware first. The middleware loads rules from the cache, and fetches counters and last request timestamp from Redis. If not rate limited, the request is forwarded to API servers. If rate limited, the middleware returns 429 to the client, and meanwhile the request is either dropped or forwarded to a message queue for later processing.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder (like 0008 stage 2). Tiles: Client, Rate limiter middleware, API servers, Redis (counters), Rules (disk), Workers, Cache (rules), Message queue, plus 2 distractors (CDN for static images, SQL database for counters). The learner taps tiles in a valid build order; each placed tile draws its arrows. Dependency rule: a tile whose upstream isn't drawn yet costs a 'minute' on a small clock; a distractor costs a heart with an explanation. Then predict-then-watch with three requests: (1) under limit → path lights Client → middleware → Redis check → API servers; (2) over limit, 'drop' mode → 429 back to client; (3) over limit, an order request with 'enqueue' mode on → 429 to client and the request goes to the queue (processed later). Learner predicts the path for each before it lights up.
stages.check: Diagram complete with no distractors; 3 path predictions; quiz: 'Why do workers copy rules into a cache?' → so the middleware doesn't read disk on every request.

stages.title: Boss: The Header Golem
stages.sub: Counters, rules and responses under pressure
stages.teaches: Mixed scenarios on the high-level and detailed design.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 5 scenarios. Examples: 'A user is locked out for days; their key has no TTL. Most likely bug?' → crash between INCR and EXPIRE / non-atomic commands; 'Ops edits a rule on disk; how does the middleware see it?' → workers pull rules into the cache periodically; 'An order request hits the limit during a sale. Best handling?' → enqueue for later processing and tell the client; 'Client gets 429 with X-Ratelimit-Retry-After: 30. Ideal client?' → wait ≥30 s with a little jitter, then retry; 'Why not keep counters in PostgreSQL?' → disk access is slow; cache gives speed and expiry.
stages.check: Boss defeated.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Narrating the detailed design.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'Walk me through what happens to one request in your rate limiter, from the client to the API server or back.' Model answer: rules in config files on disk, workers cache them; request hits middleware; middleware loads the rule from cache and the counter from Redis (INCR with EXPIRE, done atomically); under limit → forward to API servers and update the counter; over → 429 with X-Ratelimit-Limit/Remaining/Retry-After, request dropped or queued; clients cache, back off, and handle errors. Checks: rules + workers + cache; Redis with INCR/EXPIRE; 429 + at least two headers; drop vs queue.
stages.check: Self-graded drill completed.

caveats: The X-Ratelimit-* headers are a convention, not a standard, and names vary: GitHub sends x-ratelimit-limit, x-ratelimit-remaining and x-ratelimit-reset (a timestamp). The standard header for 'wait this long' is plain Retry-After (RFC 9110), and the IETF is drafting standard RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy headers.

INCR then EXPIRE as two separate commands is not atomic: a crash between them leaves a counter that never expires. Use a Lua script or a MULTI transaction, or set the TTL only when INCR returns 1 inside the same script.
The book's flow increments the counter only for allowed requests; many real implementations INCR first and then compare, which is simpler and atomic but also counts rejected attempts.
Queueing rate-limited requests only makes sense for work that can safely run later (orders, emails). For interactive reads, a fast 429 is kinder than a long hidden wait.
Lyft's ratelimit service now lives under the Envoy project (github.com/envoyproxy/ratelimit).

quests.d: Race conditions, syncing many limiters, multi-data-center speed, and monitoring
quests.goal: Your win today: you can show the read-check-write race (two requests both see 3), fix it with a Lua script or sorted set, explain why sticky sessions lose to a central Redis, discuss edge servers and eventual consistency, and say what you'd monitor and what happens when Redis dies.
quests.bookSections: Step 3 deep dive: rate limiter in a distributed environment (race condition, synchronization issue), performance optimization, monitoring; requirement 'high fault tolerance' from Step 1

stages.title: The race
stages.sub: Two requests, one counter, wrong answer
stages.teaches: Single-server is easy; scaling to many servers and threads brings two problems: race conditions and synchronization. Race condition: the limiter (1) reads the counter from Redis, (2) checks whether counter + 1 exceeds the threshold, (3) if not, increments it by 1 in Redis. If two requests read the counter (value 3) concurrently before either writes back, each increments to 4 and writes 4 — but the correct value is 5. Locks are the obvious fix but they significantly slow the system. Two common strategies: a Lua script (Redis runs a script atomically — no other command runs in the middle) and the Redis sorted set data structure (with commands in one transaction).
stages.interaction: Interleaving sim. Two lanes, Request A and Request B, each with three step buttons: Read, Check, Write. A shared Redis box shows counter = 3; limit = 4 (so only one of A/B should pass). The learner is challenged to 'Break it': click steps in an order that lets both through (e.g. Read A, Read B, Check A, Check B, Write A, Write B → counter 4, both allowed: bug). Then a toggle 'Run as Lua script' merges each lane's three steps into one atomic block; the learner can only fire A or B whole; the second one sees 4 and is rejected; counter correct. A third toggle 'Use a lock' works too but adds a visible wait bar to every request (the latency cost). Before each run, the learner predicts the final counter value and how many requests pass.
stages.check: Bug reproduced, then fixed; predictions scored; quiz: 'Why not just use a lock?' → it significantly slows the system.

stages.title: Sticky or shared?
stages.teaches: With millions of users you need several rate limiter servers. The web tier is stateless, so a client's requests can land on different limiters. If limiter 1 only knows its own counts, it has no data about what the client did through limiter 2 — the client can exceed the limit. Option 1: sticky sessions (always route a client to the same limiter) — neither scalable nor flexible. Option 2 (book's choice): a centralized data store like Redis that all limiters share.
stages.interaction: Three-mode sim. Two limiter boxes behind a load balancer; a client sends 10 requests; limit 5/min. Mode 'Local counters' (round-robin): each limiter counts 5 → all 10 pass (learner predicts the number first: 10). Mode 'Sticky sessions': all 10 go to limiter 1 → 5 pass; then the learner presses 'Limiter 1 dies' — sticky client moves to limiter 2 with a fresh count, 5 more pass, and a 'hot limiter' heat bar shows one limiter overloaded by a heavy client (not flexible, not scalable). Mode 'Central Redis': both limiters read/write one Redis counter → 5 pass regardless of routing or failures.
stages.check: Three predictions; quiz: 'Two downsides of sticky sessions per the book?' → not scalable, not flexible.

stages.title: Go to the edge
stages.teaches: Performance optimization from the book: (1) a multi-data-center setup matters because latency is high for users far away from the data center; most cloud providers build many edge server locations around the world — the book notes Cloudflare had 194 geographically distributed edge servers as of 2020. Traffic is routed to the closest edge server to cut latency. (2) Synchronize data between them with an eventual consistency model (replicas converge after a short delay; see Ch. 6's consistency models). Trade-off: with per-region counters synced eventually, a client hitting two regions at once can briefly exceed the global limit.
stages.interaction: World map calc-and-check. A user in Sydney; one central Redis in Virginia (~200 ms round trip). Q1: 'Every API call must check Redis first. Added latency per call?' → ~200 ms (accept 150–250). Toggle 'Edge counters': each region checks a local counter (~5 ms) and syncs every 1 s. Q2: 'Limit 100/min global. A client sends 100 requests to Sydney and 100 to Frankfurt in the same second, before the sync. Worst case allowed?' → 200. Learner then picks the right framing from 3 statements: 'Edge counters trade exactness for latency; acceptable for soft limits, not for hard ones' (correct).
stages.check: Two calculations + framing pick.

stages.title: Watch the gauges
stages.sub: Monitoring, and what happens when Redis dies
stages.teaches: Monitoring: after deployment, gather analytics to check the limiter is effective — is the algorithm effective, are the rules effective? If rules are too strict, many valid requests are dropped → relax them. If the limiter becomes ineffective during a sudden traffic increase like a flash sale → replace the algorithm to support burst traffic; token bucket is a good fit. Fault tolerance (from Step 1 requirements): if the limiter's Redis goes down, decide in advance whether to fail open (let traffic through, unprotected, but the product keeps working) or fail closed (reject everything, safe but an outage). The book requires that a cache failure not affect the whole system, which points toward failing open with alerts — but for security-critical limits (login attempts) failing closed may be right.
stages.interaction: Ops dashboard with three incident charts (allowed vs 429 over time, plus a support-ticket ticker). The learner diagnoses each: (1) 30% of requests 429'd on a normal Tuesday, support tickets spiking → 'rules too strict, relax them'; (2) flash sale: legitimate burst at 12:00 all rejected, then idle → 'switch to token bucket to allow bursts'; (3) Redis node goes red: learner flips a 'fail open / fail closed' switch for two endpoints — /search (fail open is right) and /login (fail closed is defensible) — and sees the consequence animation (open: traffic flows, alert fires; closed: all 503/429s).
stages.check: Three diagnoses + two fail-mode choices; quiz: 'Flash sale broke your limiter. Book's fix?' → switch to an algorithm that supports bursts, e.g. token bucket.

stages.title: Boss: The Split-Brain Swarm
stages.teaches: Mixed distributed-systems follow-ups.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with 6 scenarios. Examples: 'Two limiter threads both read 3 and write 4. Name and fix' → race condition; Lua script / atomic op; 'Client's calls land on different limiters and exceed the limit' → synchronization; central Redis; 'Interviewer: why not sticky sessions?' → not scalable, not flexible; 'Users in Asia complain the API is slow since you added the limiter' → edge/multi-DC limiting with local counters synced eventually; 'Redis cluster is down. Your checkout API should…' → fail open with alerts (high fault tolerance); 'Valid users get 429s all day' → monitoring shows rules too strict; relax them.
stages.check: Boss defeated.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Interview-ready answer for the distributed deep dive.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'You now have 50 rate limiter servers in 3 regions. What breaks, and how do you fix it?' Model answer: race on read-check-write → Lua script or sorted set so the check-and-increment is atomic (locks too slow); stateless routing means limiters disagree → shared Redis rather than sticky sessions; distance adds latency → edge/regional counters synced with eventual consistency, accepting brief overshoot; monitor dropped vs allowed and adjust rules/algorithm; decide fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down. Checks: race + atomic fix; central store vs sticky; latency/edge with the consistency trade-off; monitoring; failure mode.
stages.check: Self-graded drill completed.

caveats: The book names Lua scripts and sorted sets but doesn't spell out a sorted-set recipe. The common one (ClassDojo): in one MULTI transaction, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to drop old timestamps, ZADD the new one, ZCARD to count, EXPIRE the key. Note the transaction makes the commands run together, but the accept/reject decision happens after, so the rejected request has already been added.
A single Redis instance is itself a bottleneck and a single point of failure; real systems shard counters across a Redis cluster (keys by user) and add replicas.

Fail open vs fail closed isn't in the book's deep dive; it follows from its 'high fault tolerance' requirement and is a very common interviewer follow-up. Stripe's write-up describes making its limiters fail open.
Cloudflare's 194 edge locations was a 2020 number; it is now well over 300 cities. Point stands: limit close to the user.
Eventual consistency between regions means a global limit is approximate; if you need an exact global cap, you pay a cross-region round trip.

quests.d: Full mock interview: design a rate limiter
quests.goal: Your win today: given 'Design a rate limiter', you can run the full 4-step interview — scope with the right questions, sketch the middleware + Redis design, choose and defend an algorithm, survive the distributed and failure curveballs, and close with hard/soft limits, layers and client best practices.
quests.bookSections: Whole chapter via the book's 4-step framework: Step 1 scoping and requirements; Step 2 placement, algorithms, high-level architecture; Step 3 rules, headers, detailed design, distributed environment, performance, monitoring; Step 4 wrap-up (hard vs soft, OSI layers, client best practices)

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: Book framework: Step 1 scope (3–10 min), Step 2 high-level design and buy-in (10–15), Step 3 deep dive (10–25), Step 4 wrap-up (3–5). For this prompt the right questions are: client- or server-side? throttle by IP / user ID / other? scale? distributed? separate service or app code? inform throttled users? — producing the six requirements (accurate limiting, low latency, little memory, distributed, clear exceptions, high fault tolerance).
stages.interaction: Same mechanic as 0008 stage 1: a 45-minute game clock bar, a chat with the interviewer ('Design a rate limiter.'), the 4-step framework strip, a requirements board with 6 slots, and a deck of ~10 question cards (6 good, 4 time-wasters such as 'Which database should the API use for products?', 'How many engineers will maintain it?', 'Should the 429 page have a logo?', 'Do we need machine learning to detect bots?'). Good questions cost 1 minute and earn signal; time-wasters cost 3 minutes and signal. Stage clears when all 6 requirements are pinned. Reveal a caveat callout afterwards: the book skips back-of-the-envelope numbers for this chapter, but an interviewer may ask (e.g. 10M daily users × a few counters × ~ tens of bytes per key ≈ a few hundred MB to low GB in Redis — show the rough maths).
stages.check: All 6 requirements pinned; signal score shown.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10–15 min)
stages.teaches: High-level: client → rate limiter middleware (or API gateway) → API servers; counters in Redis using INCR/EXPIRE; over-limit → 429.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard builder like 0008 stage 2: SVG canvas; tiles Client, Rate limiter middleware, Redis, API servers (+2 distractors: 'Limiter inside the mobile app', 'Counters in MySQL'). Tapping in dependency order draws boxes and arrows; out-of-order costs a minute, a distractor costs a heart with explanation. Then an interviewer prompt in chat: 'Which algorithm?' — learner picks from the five algorithms and one of three justifications; any algorithm with a correct matching justification is accepted (e.g. token bucket + 'allows short bursts, memory efficient, used by Stripe/Amazon'; sliding window counter + 'smooths edges with two counters per key'); a mismatched justification costs signal. Then a predict quiz: 'Limit 2/s, client sends 3 in one second: what does the third get?' → 429.
stages.check: Diagram complete; algorithm + justification picked; quiz answered.

stages.title: Deep dive: the full design
stages.sub: Step 3 · rules, headers, and the detailed diagram
stages.teaches: Detailed design: rules on disk → workers → cache; middleware loads rules from cache and counters/timestamps from Redis; allowed → API servers; limited → 429 + headers (X-Ratelimit-Limit, X-Ratelimit-Remaining, X-Ratelimit-Retry-After), request dropped or sent to a message queue.
stages.interaction: Extend the stage-2 diagram: the interviewer asks 'Where do the rules live, and how does the client know it's throttled?' Learner adds tiles Rules (disk), Workers, Cache, Message queue in a valid order, and then fills a 429 response card: status + three header names chosen from 6 options (3 distractors such as 'X-Server-Load', 'X-Cache-Hit', 'Retry-Never'). Finally a technique map like 0008 stage 3: goals on the left (allow bursts, exact rolling limit, low memory per key, atomic increment, shared count across servers, low latency far away, survive Redis outage) → learner taps the technique (token bucket, sliding window log, sliding window counter, Lua script/sorted set, central Redis, edge servers + eventual consistency, fail open + alerts).
stages.check: Diagram extended; headers correct; technique map complete.

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Mixed follow-ups from every quest of the chapter.
stages.interaction: Curveball barrage like 0008 stage 4: 9 rapid scenario cards, 3 choices each; right = 1.5 game-minutes, wrong = heart + extra minute. Cards: fixed-window edge exploit (→ sliding window counter/log); race condition two threads read 3 (→ Lua script); limiters disagree (→ central Redis, not sticky sessions); Redis down (→ fail open with alerts, or fail closed for login); users far away see added latency (→ edge + eventual consistency); flash sale throttles real buyers (→ token bucket / relax rules via monitoring); office behind one NAT IP (→ key by user/API key); key without TTL locks user out (→ atomic INCR+EXPIRE); burst of old requests starving new ones (→ that's leaking bucket; switch or shrink queue).
stages.check: Barrage completed with at least one heart left (engine rules).

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: Book's wrap-up talking points: hard vs soft rate limiting (hard: never exceed the threshold; soft: may exceed briefly); rate limiting at different levels — this design is application level (HTTP, OSI layer 7), but you can limit by IP with iptables at layer 3; avoid being rate limited as a client — client cache, know the limit, catch errors and recover gracefully, enough back-off in retries. Also good closers: recap the design and its bottlenecks (Redis as single point of failure, approximate global limits).
stages.interaction: Like 0008 stage 5: 7 closing-move cards; the learner picks exactly 3 and presses 'Deliver my close'. Good cards: 'Hard vs soft limits and which this is', 'Layer 7 here, layer 3 with iptables for floods', 'Client best practices: cache, back off with jitter, handle 429', 'Name the bottleneck: Redis — shard it, add replicas, decide fail-open'. Weak cards: 'Say: I think we're done', 'Re-explain the token bucket from scratch', 'Propose rewriting it in a new language'. Score depends on how many strong cards are picked; interviewer chat reacts to each.
stages.check: Close delivered with at least 2 strong moves.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.teaches: Whole-chapter recap.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: 'In 60 seconds: design a rate limiter.' Model answer: scope (server-side, flexible rules by user/IP, distributed, inform users, fault tolerant); middleware or API gateway in front of API servers; algorithm choice with trade-off (token bucket for bursts or sliding window counter for smooth, cheap accuracy); counters in Redis with atomic INCR/EXPIRE or Lua; rules in config files cached by workers; 429 + rate-limit headers, drop or queue; distributed: atomic ops for races, central Redis for sync, edge + eventual consistency for latency; monitor and tune; fail open on cache outage. Checks: scoping; placement; algorithm + trade-off; Redis + atomicity; 429/headers; one distributed issue; one failure mode. Then a scorecard (minutes used, signal, hearts) saved under its own localStorage key (e.g. 'sdq:v1:ch4-boss-interview'), mirroring 0008's separate key.
stages.check: Self-graded drill completed; scorecard shown.

caveats: The minute ranges are the book's suggestion for a roughly 45-minute session; real loops vary.
The book's rate limiter chapter has no back-of-the-envelope estimation; be ready to do rough Redis memory and QPS maths if asked.
There is no single right algorithm. Interviewers reward a choice tied to a stated requirement (bursts allowed? exactness needed? memory budget?), not a particular name.
The X-Ratelimit-* header names are a convention, not a standard (see 4.4).

cheatsheetOutline: One page, 'World 4 — Rate Limiter'. Header strip: the 4-step framework with minute ranges. Section 4.1 Why & where: definition; 3 benefits (DoS/starvation, cost, overload) with book example limits; 6 scoping questions → 6 requirements; placement (client unreliable; middleware; API gateway features); build-vs-buy guidelines; L7 vs L3 (iptables). Section 4.2 Buckets: token bucket (size + refill rate; book fig 4 tokens, 4/min; lazy refill formula tokens = min(cap, tokens + Δt × rate); buckets per rule per key; global bucket 10,000 rps; Amazon/Stripe) vs leaking bucket (FIFO queue size + outflow rate; Shopify; old requests starve new); hard vs soft limits. Section 4.3 Windows: fixed window (5/min → 10 in 2:00:30–2:01:30), sliding log (book timestamps 1:00:01 / 1:00:30 / 1:00:50 rejected-but-logged / 1:01:40 accepted; Redis sorted set; memory cost), sliding window counter (current + previous × overlap; 3 + 5 × 0.7 = 6.5 → 6 < 7; Cloudflare 0.003% of 400M). Five-algorithm comparison table (pro / con / who uses it). Section 4.4 Counter room: Redis INCR + EXPIRE (atomic!), Lyft YAML rule examples (5 marketing msgs/day; 5 logins/min), 429 + X-Ratelimit-Limit / -Remaining / -Retry-After (and standard Retry-After), drop vs queue, client best practices (cache, know limits, handle errors, back off with jitter). Section 4.5 Distributed: race (both read 3, write 4; fix Lua script / sorted set, locks too slow), sync (sticky sessions bad, central Redis good), multi-DC/edge + eventual consistency (latency vs exactness), monitoring (rules too strict → relax; flash sale → token bucket), fail open vs fail closed. Key numbers box: 429; 2 req/s example; 4-token bucket; 10,000 rps global bucket; 5/min edge → 10; 7/min sliding counter example; 0.003% / 400M; 194 Cloudflare edge locations (2020). Final design diagram: Rules (disk) → Workers → Cache; Client → Rate limiter middleware ↔ Redis (counters) → API servers; limited → 429 to client + drop or Message queue. Footer: honest caveats list (non-standard headers, leaky-bucket meter vs queue, INCR/EXPIRE atomicity, approximate global limits, fail-open choice).
